notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Plates are entirely white with black text and no blue EU strip on the left.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Cyrillic script with the special letters Ы, Э, Ё and Ъ. Ё also shows up in Mongolian, Ъ in Bulgarian.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Street is улица (ул.) and city is город (г.). Ukraine instead uses вулиця and місто.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Three bollard types: a very thin one on a stick, one with a black top and a red vertical reflector below, and a German-style one.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Intersections tend to be very wide and packed with a large number of bollards.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signposts often have a black-painted lower section.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Mostly square concrete utility poles, also seen across other ex-Soviet countries.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Concrete support blocks at the foot of utility poles, often lifting wooden poles off the ground.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Black and white striped pole shields are common along highways, especially in the western part.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs show a simply drawn person over three stripes, often with a bright yellow border.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Pedestrian crossings use alternating white and yellow stripes.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Black and white striped guardrails, kerbs and bridge barriers are common.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Cities are full of large, plain, rectangular concrete apartment blocks; newer buildings in rich areas look more modern.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Rural homes are mostly simple wooden structures with metal roofs.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Richly carved window frames, often painted blue, mark traditional wooden houses.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Heating pipes run above ground, held up by vertical pipes in towns.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Common older camera cars are a black and a white one with a long antenna, or a short antenna with no visible car.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Dense birch stands and birch-only forests point east of the Urals, mostly between Chelyabinsk and Novosibirsk.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Siberian larches dominate more and more the further east you go, and at high elevation.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Lots of pink fireweed suggests the north, and most areas north of the capital.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sunflower fields are common near the Ukrainian border and in eastern oblasts like Samara and Ulyanovsk.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Giant butterbur leaves are very common in southern Sakhalin.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Oaks with a white stripe painted round the trunk are extremely common here.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Grey gravelly soil and many volcanoes close to the road mark this peninsula.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Extremely dry, flat land west of the Caspian Sea: Kalmykia, Astrakhan and Dagestan.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Open grassland with shrubs and mountains, lusher around Lake Baikal.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Green farm fields broken by isolated birch patches, usually summer coverage.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rocks along the roadside are extremely common across Karelia and Murmansk.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Unblurred plates end with a regional code; codes run alphabetically, republics first (01 Adygea, 23 Krasnodar). Three digits use the last two.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Japanese right-hand-drive cars become common the further east you go, from around Novosibirsk.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: The very thin bollard on a stick is mostly found from around Omsk eastward.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Some republics have bilingual town signs, such as Tatar in Tatarstan and Bashkir in Bashkortostan.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Town names written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters are common near the Baltic border and around the capital.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Brown tourist-attraction signs are common in the capital region and the oblasts around it.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: White limestone brick buildings point to Dagestan and neighbouring regions.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Mosques are most common in the Muslim-majority south, Tatarstan and Bashkortostan.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Clips on the edges of signposts are found in the Saint Petersburg and Leningrad area.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Yellow plates fixed by a metal band appear on most poles in Tatarstan.
